title: Mura and His Seven Sons
story:
Narakasura, the demon king of Pragjyotisha, had robbed the treasury of heaven itself, and Krishna had come to end his reign. Mountains walled the demon's city, forts bristled with weapons, belts of fire and water ringed every approach, and snares hung where no eye could see them — and Krishna had broken them all, one after another, riding Garuda, the great eagle, with his wife Satyabhama at his side. Only one defense was left, and it lay in the deep water beneath the citadel. There, as the last echoes of the assault died away, the city's guardian opened his eyes.

Mura, the five-headed guardian of the water, rose from the deep, and the water fell from him in sheets. All five of his heads roared at once — a roar like fire and thunder together — and in his hand he swung a trident. He hurled it at Krishna with all his might: a spear so fierce that no eye could rest on it, flung to end the assault before it could reach the citadel.

Krishna did not so much as move. Two arrows met the trident in mid-air and broke it, and the three-pronged weapon fell harmless to the ground.

Mura's mace came next, and Krishna shattered it in turn, the great club bursting into a thousand splinters as though it had been made of dry wood. Then Krishna's discus flew, and where it passed, the five heads of Mura were cut away, one after another. The guardian who had slept in the waters of Pragjyotisha fell back into them — lifeless, like a mountain whose peaks have been sheared off by a thunderbolt. The waters closed over him, and for a moment the citadel was quiet: the quiet after a city has watched its defenses fall in a single morning.

But Mura had sons — seven of them: Tamra, Antariksha, Sravana, Vibhavasu, Vasu, Nabhasvan, and Aruna. They had watched their father die, and they came out of the fortress with every weapon they could carry — arrows and swords, maces and spears, javelins, tridents, and lances. They came out not as an army but as a family: seven brothers with everything they had, driven by grief and rage, flinging themselves at the one who had slain their father.

Krishna met them as he had met their father. One after another he brought them down, until all seven lay beside Mura before the citadel, and Pragjyotisha had no defenders left.

From the heights of the citadel, Narakasura watched it all: Krishna upon Garuda, Satyabhama at his side. In his desperation the demon king hurled his last weapon — the sataghni, the hundred-killer — and all his warriors loosed their shafts at once, the whole fury of the city's last stand breaking against the rider on the great bird.

The hundred-killer flew, and the arrows flew, and when the air cleared, the rider was still there — and the master of the citadel knew that nothing he owned could stop what was coming.
reflection: Mura's sons come out to avenge their father and are destroyed in the same motion of love and rage; the loyalty that makes them memorable is precisely what kills them. The episode shows resistance falling in layers — guardian, sons, then the king's last weapon — until nothing stands between Krishna and the citadel but the citadel's master.
content_note: Contains the slaying of the demon Mura and his seven sons; described with restraint and no gore.
next_story_tease: Nothing now stood between Krishna and the citadel but Narakasura himself.
